To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

ethanol produced from sugarcane and corn stover has the largest energy and GHG benefits among all five bioethanol feedstocks, with ethanol from miscanthus having the greatest benefits of all five feedstocks.

the energy use and GHGs from using bioethanols made from corn, sugcane, corn stoves, switchgrass and misanthus are 19‐48% (corn), 40‐62% (sugarcane), 90‐103% (corn stover), 77‐97 (switchgrass) and 101‐ 115% (misanthus) less than the fossil fuel equivalent.

ethanol from corn, switchgrass, sugarcane (with and without co-product credits), and miscanthus (with and without coproduct credits), can reduce life-cycle greenhouse gas emissions by 19%, 77%, 40% to 62%, 77% to 97% and 100% to 114%, respectively, relative to the use of petroleum gasoline, and that ethanol from corn stover can reduce greenhouse gas emissions by up to 102%, relative to petroleum gasoline.

the use of bioethanol made with the five feedstocks can help reduce both life-cycle energy use and GHGs from using transportation fuels, with the greatest reductions from using cellulosic biomass.

, relative to petroleum gasoline, bioethanol from corn, sug cane, corn stover and cellulosic feedstock can reduce fossil energy use and GHGs emissions, and that bioethanol from sugarcane and from cellulosic feedstocks can achieve greater reductions than bioethanol from grain corn.

the life-cycle energy use and GHGs emissions of bioethanol can be significantly improved through the use of more efficient feedstock production, conversion technologies and feedstock sources.
